Movement artifacts were removed using temporal principal component analysis (PCA) with a promax rotation that identifies factors accounting for amplitude differences greater than 200μV within a trial (Dien, 2010). Channels with an absolute correlation with the nearest six neighboring channels that fell below .4 were marked as globally bad. On a trial-wise basis, channels with a voltage range exceeding 100μV within an epoch, channels that were flat, and channels with more than a 30μV difference with the nearest six neighbors were marked as bad for the epoch. Channels that were marked as bad for more than 20% of epochs were considered globally bad. Bad channels were interpolated using spherical splines (Perrin et al., 1989), but if more than 10% of channels were marked bad for an epoch, the entire epoch was rejected. Participants were excluded if fewer than six error trials were retained after artifact correction and rejection, consistent with the exclusion criteria used in the parent study (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).

Response-locked ERPs were baseline adjusted using a time window from 400ms to 200ms before the participant's response. ERN was quantified at the trial level using a timewindow mean amplitude from 0 to 100ms following participant response at electrode site 6 (FCz). Pe was similarly quantified at the trial level using a time-window mean amplitude from 200 to 400ms at electrode 62 (Pz).

Data Analysis

Multilevel models were used to examine relationships between trial-level ERP scores and behavior. For RT, MLSMs were used to model both mean RT and RT variability. For accuracy, multilevel Bernoulli outcome models were used because accuracy was binary. MLSMs facilitate the examination of average scores (location portion of the model) and within-person variance (scale portion of the model; the scale portion modeled standard deviations using a log link).

These models have been successfully implemented in studies of trial-level ERP scores (Clayson, Brush, et al., 2021; Clayson et al., 2022; Clayson, Shuford, et al., 2024). By relaxing the assumption of a homogeneous variance structure, MLSMs support the modeling of residual variance as a function of covariates, which is essential for testing the proposed hypotheses. The proposed analyses examined the same predictors on the location and scale portions of the model.

Predictors on the location portion of the model aimed to clarify the degree to which previoustrial ERN amplitude, previous-trial Pe amplitude, and internalizing or externalizing symptoms predicted current-trial behavior. Predictors on the scale portion of the model aimed to clarify the degree to which predictors accounted for changes in the variability of behavior.

The models for testing each hypothesis are described below using Wilkinson notation (Wilkinson & Rogers, 1973). In the following notation, Behavior represents either current-trial RT or accuracy, depending on the model, and ERN and Pe represent ERP component amplitudes from the previous trial. Internalizing and Externalizing represent the composite scores centered on each dimension for the given individual. Random effects were included for Previous Trial and Subject to account for ERP component amplitudes being nested within previous trials, which were nested within participants. Of note, all interaction effects include lower-order constituent main effects. Separate models were used to examine RTs and accuracy.

Data were included in the trial-level models only when the previous trial had ERP component scores retained and the current trial had valid behavioral data (i.e., a response was required for the RT analysis; trials with no response were retained in the accuracy analysis and coded as errors). The first trial of each block was excluded because it did not have a preceding trial.

Hypothesis 1. This model parallels the typical analysis of post-error behavioral adjustments and helps to determine whether previous-trial ERP components relate to current-trial behavior, ignoring any effect of psychiatric symptoms. Previous-trial accuracy (Rabbitt & Rodgers, 1977) and current-trial congruency (Kornblum et al., 1990) were included to account for the effect of experimental conditions and previous-trial performance that may impact currenttrial behavior. Exploratory Analysis. Exploratory model comparisons were conducted to identify the combination of previous-trial ERP component amplitudes, symptoms, and interaction variables that best predicted current-trial RT and accuracy. To limit the model search space, all candidate models included current-trial congruency and previous-trial accuracy. Candidate models then varied in whether they included previous-trial ERN, previous-trial Pe, Internalizing, Externalizing, and the theoretically relevant ERP-symptom interactions. Models were constructed such that interaction terms always included their lower-order terms. The same fixed-effect structure was used in the location and scale portions of RT models. A total of 47 candidate models was evaluated for each outcome. using the package brms v2.20.4 (Bürkner, 2017), which is a front-end wrapper for Stan (Stan Development Team, 2021). For the models with RTs as the dependent variable, the prior for the intercept on the location portion of the model used a normal distribution with a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100, and the priors for the fixed effects used a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 100. Variance components were estimated using a Student's t prior distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, a location parameter of 0, and a scale parameter of 2. A Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe (LKJ) prior distribution with a shape parameter of 2 was used as the prior for the correlation matrices of the group-level effects (Lewandowski et al., 2009). The prior is defined over positive-definite correlation matrices for the group-level effects. A shape = 2 parameter can be considered mildly informative, placing more weight on an identity matrix.

For the model with accuracy as the dependent variable, Bayesian location-only multilevel models with Bernoulli outcomes (0 [error], 1 [correct]) were used and fit with a logit link. In such analyses, there was no scale portion of the model to estimate. A flat prior was used for the population-level intercept and population-level regression coefficients. An LKJ prior distribution with a shape parameter of 1 was used as the prior for the correlation between the varying intercepts, and a shape = 1 parameter can be considered a uniform prior.

Model Comparisons.

Leave-one-out cross-validation via Pareto smoothed importance sampling (LOO-CV) was used to compare model fit using the loo package in R (Vehtari et al., 2017). Model comparisons were performed using LOO-CV, which compares the predictive accuracy of the models. The following criteria were used to identify the optimal model. 1) The difference in expected log predictive density was greater than 4.2) The difference in expected log predictive density was greater than 2 times the standard error of the difference in expected log predictive density. When the above criteria did not identify a single best-fitting model, the model with the fewest predictors among those not distinguishable from the model with the highest expected log predictive density under these criteria was selected. When model comparison did not favor a more complex model, parameter estimates from that model were treated as descriptive and were not interpreted as robust evidence for the corresponding hypothesis.

Test of Hypotheses

The first hypothesis would be supported if the 95% credible intervals (CrIs) of the posterior samples for the 1) parameter estimates of previous-trial ERN were negative and excluded 0 and 2) parameter estimates of previous-trial Pe were positive and excluded 0 for the model predicting current-trial RTs and the model predicting current-trial accuracy. This finding would support the conclusion that greater (i.e., more negative) previous-trial ERN and larger (i.e., more positive) previous-trial Pe predict longer RTs and improved current-trial accuracy.

The second hypothesis would be supported 1) if Model 2 showed improved model fit over Model 1 using LOO-CV and 2) if the 95% CrIs of the posterior samples for the parameter estimates of the interaction effects (ERN x Internalizing, ERN x Externalizing, Pe x Internalizing, Pe x Externalizing) excluded 0 for the model predicting current-trial RTs and the model predicting current-trial accuracy; the parameter estimates for the interaction effects should be in the direction toward smaller effects (e.g., positive estimates for interactions with ERN and negative estimates for interactions with Pe). This finding would support the conclusion that greater psychiatric symptom scores are associated with weaker relationships between previoustrial error-monitoring ERPs and current-trial behavior.

For the exploratory analysis, models were compared using LOO-CV, and the optimal model was identified using the rules described in the Model Comparison section. If multiple models show the best predictive accuracy with the same number of predictors, the model with the numerically best expected log predictive density (i.e., least negative expected log predictive density) was selected as the optimal model for further interpretation.

Results

Descriptive Statistics of ERP Scores and Behavioral Data

Demographic information is presented in Table 2, and descriptive statistics of the ERP components and behavioral data are presented in Table 3. Grand-averaged waveforms and the topographical maps are shown in Figure 1. All models reported below showed satisfactory congrence (𝑅 ̂ < 1.01), and visual inspection of traceplots indicated adequate mixing.

RT Models Hypothesis 1. The parameter estimates of the RT model for Hypothesis 1 are presented in Table 4. A larger previous-trial ERN (i.e., more negative) predicted longer current-trial RTs but did not predict current-trial RT variability (location 95% credible interval [CrI] [-.17, -.03]; scale 95% CrI [-.002, 0.00003]).

Specifically, each 1-µV increase in previous-trial ERN (i.e., a more negative ERN) was associated with a current-trial RT that was 0.10 ms longer. In contrast, larger previous-trial Pe (i.e., more positive) predicted neither current-trial RT nor its variability (location 95% CrI [-.07, 0.06]; scale 95% CrI [-.001, 0.0002]).

With respect to the experimental effects, RT was longer and more variable following error trials than correct trials (location 95% CrI [-17.25, -11.99]; scale 95% CrI [-.12, -.07]) and on current-incongruent trials than on current-congruent trials (location 95% CrI [-45.85, -40.49]; scale 95% CrI [-.23, -.19]). In other words, RT was 14.57 ms longer when the previous trial was an error trial than when it was a correct trial; likewise, RT was 43.25 ms longer when the current trial was incongruent than congruent.

Overall, previous-trial ERN, but not Pe, predicted current-trial RT. Therefore, Hypothesis 1 was partially supported for RT. The effects of previous-trial ERN on current-trial RT and its variability are demonstrated in Figures 2 and 3, respectively.

Hypothesis 2. The parameter estimates of the RT model for Hypothesis 2 are presented in Table 5. The model comparisons indicated that the model from Hypothesis 2 (i.e., model including the moderating role of psychiatric symptom scores) showed comparable fit to the model from Hypothesis 1 (i.e., without psychiatric symptom scores; differences in 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= -1.24, SEs of 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑓 ̂= 4.64). Therefore, the more parsimonious model for Hypothesis 1 was interpreted, and Hypothesis 2 was not supported.

Exploratory Analysis.

A total of 47 RT models were compared. The LOO-CV comparison identified seven models that met the prespecified model-comparison criteria, which included the model from Hypothesis 1. Among the seven models, the model from Hypothesis 1 included the fewest predictors and was consequently selected as the best-fitting model (i.e., ∆𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= -1.24, SE of ∆𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= 4.64). The model interpretation is identical to that provided for the model in Hypothesis 1.

Taken together, exploratory RT models provided consistent evidence that more negative previous-trial ERN amplitudes predicted longer current-trial RTs. Symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy in the exploratory model-comparison framework, suggesting that ERP-RT relationships were broadly similar across levels of internalizing and externalizing symptom scores. Interim Summary. In summary, the RT models consistently showed that larger previous-trial ERN amplitudes predicted longer current-trial RTs. Previous-trial Pe did not robustly predict current-trial RT or RT variability. Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not meaningfully predict RT and did not provide robust evidence of moderation of ERP-RT associations. Thus, Hypothesis 1 was partially supported for RT, and Hypothesis 2 was not supported. The plots demonstrating the interactions between previous-trial ERPs and psychiatric symptom scores on current-trial RT are included in the supplementary materials. Accuracy Models Hypothesis 1. Parameter estimates of the accuracy model for Hypothesis 1 are presented in Table 6. Larger previous-trial Pe predicted higher odds of a correct response on the current trial (odds ratio [OR] = 1.003, 95% CrI [1.0002, 1.005]; accuracy-model estimates are reported on the log-odds scale). In other words, for each 1-µV increase in previous-trial Pe, the odds of observing a correct response on the subsequent trial increased by approximately 0.3%. Previoustrial ERN did not predict current-trial accuracy (95% CrI [-.005, 0.001]). Current-trial congruency predicted current-trial accuracy: accuracy was higher on congruent than incongruent trials, and the odds of a correct response were approximately 5.4 times greater on congruent than incongruent trials (OR = 5.40; 95% CrI [4.81, 6.17]). Previous-trial accuracy did not predict current-trial accuracy (95% CrI [-.15, 0.11]). Thus, Hypothesis 1 was partially supported for accuracy: previous-trial Pe, but not ERN, predicted current-trial accuracy. The effect of previous-trial Pe on current-trial accuracy is demonstrated in Figure 4. Hypothesis 2. The parameter estimates of the accuracy model for Hypothesis 2 are presented in Table 7. The model comparisons indicated that the model from Hypothesis 1 (i.e., without psychiatric symptom scores) showed indistinguishable fit compared to the model from Hypothesis 2 (i.e., the model including the moderating role of psychiatric symptom scores), while including fewer predictors (differences in 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= -2.83, SEs of differences in 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= 1.52).

Therefore, the model from Hypothesis 1 was preferred, and Hypothesis 2 was not supported.

Exploratory Analysis.

A total of 47 accuracy models were compared. Although LOO-CV reduces the risk of selecting an overfit model by evaluating out-of-sample predictive performance, comparing a large number of candidate models in this exploratory analysis increases the possibility that the selected model capitalized on characteristics of the present data.

Therefore, the selected model should be interpreted cautiously, and its findings require independent replication in future studies. Parameter estimates for the selected exploratory model are presented in Taken together, most predictors in the selected exploratory model had 95% credible intervals that included zero. It is important to note that LOO-CV evaluates the predictive performance of the model as a whole rather than the evidence for individual parameters. Hence, the selected model had the best out-of-sample predictive performance among the candidate models, even though there was limited posterior support for the associations between the individual predictors and current-trial accuracy.

Correlations Among Symptom Scores, ERP Amplitudes, and Behavioral Measures

Exploratory frequentist bivariate correlations using participant-level summary scores were conducted among symptom scores, ERP component amplitudes, and behavioral measures (see Tables 9 and 10). ASR internalizing and externalizing symptom scores were positively correlated with each other, r(245) = .55, p < .001, but were not significantly correlated with ERP component amplitudes (|rs| ≤ .11, ps > .05).

Discussion

The present study examined whether previous-trial performance-monitoring ERP components predicted current-trial behavior and whether these relationships were moderated by self-reported psychiatric symptom severity. Larger previous-trial ERN predicted longer currenttrial mean RTs, and larger previous-trial Pe predicted greater odds of a correct current-trial response in the confirmatory model. In confirmatory analyses, internalizing and externalizing symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy or provide robust evidence of moderation.

Internalizing and externalizing symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy or provide robust evidence of moderation. Taken together, these findings provide no robust evidence that broad ASR internalizing or externalizing symptom scores disrupted trial-level ERP-behavior coupling.

Trial-Level ERP-Behavior Relationships

ERN-RT relationships were observed across different RT models, such that larger ERN (i.e., more negative) on the previous trial predicted longer mean RTs on the current trial. This pattern of effects suggests that a heightened neural response to errors is associated with slower responding on the subsequent trial. This relationship between larger ERN and longer RT is broadly consistent with other work (Carp & Compton, 2009; Hajcak et al., 2003; Mattes et al., 2022; Park et al., 2024; Schroder et al., 2020). However, ERN-RT associations without meaningful ERN-accuracy associations at the trial level challenge the cognitive control account of the ERN, which holds that it reflects increased cognitive control following an error, thereby supporting the remedial action of error commission (Botvinick et al., 2001; Falkenstein et al., 1991; Gehring et al., 1993; Yeung et al., 2004). One of the prevailing accounts of post-error slowing posits that the delayed response may stem from momentary inhibition of ongoing motor activity or from heightened error processing that interferes with the reorientation of attention to the current trial (Houtman & Notebaert, 2013; Lavro et al., 2018; Wessel, 2018). For instance, such interference may impact encoding of the current-trial stimulus, which further impedes engagement with the current trial (Buzzell et al., 2017; Notebaert et al., 2009). A pattern of longer RT following errors and an association between more negative previous-trial ERN amplitudes and longer current-trial RTs is consistent with orienting or interference accounts.

However, the absence of a clear ERN-accuracy relationship does not conclusively indicate that slowing was maladaptive or distinguish these accounts from adaptive adjustments.

It is important to note that the interpretation of post-error slowing and the ERN varies with the specifics of the experimental paradigms used. Specifically, ERN amplitude is sensitive to prolonged task performance (Clayson, Baldwin, et al., 2025). Similarly, larger ERN was found under experimental conditions where accuracy was emphasized over speed (Mattes et al., 2023).

The interpretation of post-error slowing also differs across task specifications, especially with respect to the response-stimulus interval (RSI). Specifically, Wessel (2018) explains that posterror slowing during experimental paradigms with longer RSI may reflect increased caution, whereas post-error slowing during paradigms with shorter RSI may better reflect reorientation of attention following disengagement from an error. In summary, the present findings leave the functional significance of the ERN-RT association unresolved. Examination of ERN-RT relationships across different experimental paradigms might help clarify the role of the errormonitoring process indexed by the ERN in the context of post-error behavioral adjustments.

In the confirmatory model, larger previous-trial Pe predicted greater odds of a correct response on the current trial. However, this association was not retained as a robust effect in the exploratory model-comparison framework, so the Pe-accuracy finding should be interpreted cautiously. The Pe coefficient remained positive in the exploratory model, but its 95% credible interval included zero. Because that model included a Pe × Internalizing interaction, its Pe coefficient represented the association at a centered internalizing score of zero. On the other hand, previous-trial ERN did not predict current-trial accuracy in any of the models. Taken together, considering that ERN reflects rapid, automatic error detection that can trigger behavioral adjustment, whereas Pe reflects later conscious error awareness that may support a more strategic behavioral adjustment, it is plausible that deeper error processing, as indexed by a larger Pe, predicts improved accuracy in line with the task goal (Di Gregorio et al., 2018; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001; Steinhauser & Yeung, 2010). However, this functional interpretation remains tentative because evidence for a robust Pe-accuracy association was not consistent across model specifications.

Taken together, the findings are consistent with partially dissociable ERP-behavior associations, with the most robust evidence for an association between previous-trial ERN and current-trial RT. Evidence for a Pe-accuracy association was more model-dependent. Future work incorporating drift-diffusion modeling could clarify whether ERN-related RT slowing reflects increased response caution, changes in nondecision time, reduced processing efficiency, or other decision-related mechanisms (Grabowska et al., 2025; Mattes et al., 2022; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008). Examining the relationship between previous-trial ERPs and current-trial driftdiffusion model paramters could clarify how error-related neural activity relates to changes in response styles or efficiency of extracting information.

Moderating Role of Psychiatric Symptoms in ERP-Behavior Relationships

In confirmatory analyses, psychiatric symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy under the prespecified model-comparison criteria, and the exploratory models did not provide robust evidence that symptom scores predicted behavior or moderated ERP-behavior associations. These findings do not establish equivalent ERP-behavior relationships across symptom levels. Supplemental recruitment broadened the observed internalizing range but did not comparably extend the externalizing range. Limited representation of high externalizing scores may have reduced sensitivity to moderation and constrained generalization to populations with elevated externalizing symptoms. Therefore, further investigation in samples spanning a broader distribution of externalizing severity is needed to determine whether externalizing symptoms show a moderating ERP-behavior effect.

Despite the limited literature on the ERP-behavior relationships in psychopathology, the present finding is consistent with a recent study that examined ERP-behavior relationships in people with psychosis and healthy comparison participants, where intact trial-level ERP-RT relationships were observed in both groups despite overall blunted ERPs in the psychosis group (Park et al., 2025). Taken together, the findings do not support the hypothesis that broad symptom severity disrupts these trial-level associations within the observed symptom range. This is notable because studies in individuals with high internalizing or externalizing symptom severity often focused on symptom-or group-related differences in ERP component amplitudes (Lutz et al., 2021; Pasion & Barbosa, 2019; Riesel et al., 2017), whereas the present study tested whether symptom severity altered trial-level associations between ERP amplitudes and subsequent behavior. In the present sample, however, exploratory participant-level correlations did not clearly reproduce typical symptom-ERP amplitude patterns, which may be due to differences in symptom breadth, task context, or scoring conventions.

The null findings for the moderating role of psychiatric symptoms may partly reflect the broad nature of the symptom measures used in the present study. Atypical ERP-RT relationships might be more strongly related to specific symptom dimensions than to broad symptom clusters.

For example, although large ERN is often observed in internalizing psychopathology, potentiated ERN is typically observed in the context of OCD (Bellato et al., 2021; Hajcak et al., 2019; Riesel, 2019; Riesel et al., 2017), whereas findings in depression are mixed (Clayson et al., 2020; Hajcak et al., 2025; Klawohn et al., 2020; Weinberg et al., 2012). Similarly, studies of behavioral measures suggest that changes in post-error RT might be more specific to particular disorders or symptoms than to broad internalizing symptoms (Rueppel et al., 2022). One possibility is that ERP-behavior abnormalities are more closely tied to specific symptom profiles, diagnoses, or information-processing styles than to broad internalizing and externalizing composite scores (Kotov et al., 2021). Future studies that directly sample these profiles are needed to test this possibility. For instance, future studies could compare validated hierarchical symptom models that distinguish shared psychopathology from more specific symptom dimensions (Caspi et al., 2014). Such analyses would require evaluation of the measurement structure and the psychometric reliability and interpretation of the resulting factors. The extraction of a general factor should not be assumed to reveal ERP-behavior relationships obscured by composite scores.

Taken together, the findings provide no robust evidence that broad internalizing or externalizing symptom scores moderated ERP-behavior associations in this undergraduate sample. However, because clinical diagnoses were not evaluated in this sample, it is possible that findings would differ in a clinical sample. Additionally, given the high comorbidity of psychopathology and the limited specificity captured by broad symptom clusters, future studies might examine different symptom profiles or maladaptive information processing styles that are closely tied to impaired cognitive control (Koster et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2000; Owens et al., 2021; Owens et al., 2025).

Limitations and Future Directions

The present study is not without its limitations. First, the undergraduate sampling frame and supplemental recruitment strategy constrained the range and distribution of psychiatric symptom severity, particularly for externalizing symptoms. Despite this limitation, the present study identified a robust trial-level ERN-RT relationship. Replication in clinical populations is important to clarify how the performance monitoring system might be perturbed across varying levels and profiles of psychiatric symptom severity.

Second, ERP-behavior relationships were examined only during a flanker task. Neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring, as well as their interrelationships, are known to show task-specific effects (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025; Clayson et al., 2022; Park et al., 2024). Therefore, specific psychiatric symptom scores might play a role in the relationship between ERPs and behavior measured during other experimental tasks, as these measures in isolation appear to have different relations to measures of psychiatric symptoms across tasks (Gillan et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2021; Weinberg et al., 2015). Moreover, given that different information processing styles appear associated with impaired cognitive control in psychopathology (i.e., reflective rumination vs. depressive rumination; Koster et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2000; Owens et al., 2021; Owens et al., 2025), the perturbed link between performance monitoring ERPs and behavior might be more pronounced when assessed during experimental tasks that target specific psychological processes of interest (e.g., social reward task, Distefano et al., 2018; Balloon Analogue Risk Task, Lejuez et al., 2002).

Because the most consistent and robust effects emerged for RT, computational decomposition of RTs may provide mechanistic insight into which aspects of decision processing are related to error-monitoring ERP components. RT is measured at the end of multiple layers of cognitive processes involved in decision making. As a result, analyses of raw RT may provide only a coarse index of how error monitoring relates to subsequent goal-directed behavior (Dutilh et al., 2011; Weindel et al., 2021). Drift diffusion modeling (DDM) is a computational model that facilitates decomposing RT into different cognitive parameters, such as response caution, response bias, and efficiency of information processing (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; Smith & Ratcliff, 2024). Given the preserved ERP-RT relationships observed in the present study and in other work on psychopathology (Park et al., 2025), linking error-monitoring ERPs from the previous trial to DDM parameters on the subsequent trial may help clarify how the errormonitoring system differentially drives behavioral adjustment across levels and types of psychiatric symptoms.

Last, the reported models also did not explicitly include trial-number trends or serially correlated residuals. Consequently, the extent to which slow changes in attention, fatigue, or performance contributed to the lagged ERP-behavior associations remains unresolved. Future studies might examine the role of the number of trials and task duration to delineate how ERPbehavior relations change over time, especially as a function of fatigue or habituation.

Despite these limitations, the present study had many strengths. First, the sample size was relatively large for an EEG study (Clayson et al., 2019; Lakens, 2022). Second, the use of triallevel multilevel models facilitated examination of within-person associations between performance-monitoring ERP component amplitudes and subsequent behavior, allowing the study to test lagged, within-person ERP-behavior associations rather than relying on participantlevel averages. As such, the present study provides a foundation for studies that examine the dynamic relationships among different subcomponents of performance monitoring, and more broadly, cognitive control, by integrating multiple neural and behavioral measurements at the trial level.

Conclusion

Interim

Summary. Thus, the confirmatory Hypothesis 1 model provided evidence that larger previous-trial Pe predicted higher current-trial accuracy, but this association was not retained as a robust effect in the exploratory model-comparison framework. Internalizing and externalizing symptoms did not robustly moderate ERP-accuracy relationships. The plots demonstrating the interactions between previous-trial ERPs and psychiatric symptom scores on current-trial accuracy are included in the supplementary materials.

present study tested whether trial-level performance-monitoring ERP component amplitudes predicted subsequent behavior and whether these associations varied across broad internalizing and externalizing symptom scores. Larger previous-trial ERN amplitudes predicted longer current-trial mean RTs, suggesting that stronger early error-monitoring activity was associated with slower responding on the next trial. Larger previous-trial Pe amplitudes predicted greater odds of a correct current-trial response in the confirmatory model. Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not provide robust evidence of moderation, indicating that broad ASR symptom severity did not robustly alter trial-level ERP-behavior associations within the observed symptom range of this undergraduate sample. These findings highlight the value of examining performance monitoring as a trial-level neural-behavioral process rather than relying only on isolated ERP or behavioral averages.
